Text Description: A retail store operates a complex supply chain to distribute products across various categories, serving customers in multiple geographic regions. The daily demand of customer groups is recorded in "customer_demand.csv", while the supply capacity of distribution centers is detailed in "supply_capacity.csv". The transportation cost per unit of goods from each distribution center to each customer group is recorded in "transportation_costs.csv". The objective is to develop an optimal fulfillment policy that determines how goods should be allocated from distribution centers to customer groups, ensuring that all demands are met without exceeding supply capacities, while minimizing the total transportation cost.

This supermarket offers a variety of best-selling products, and the specific revenue information is shown in the table, with relevant data provided in the "Revenue" column. Each product has its own demand level. The retailer"s objective is to maximize the total revenue by focusing on the sales volume of "4U" products (i.e., items with names containing "4U"). The initial inventory levels of these products are detailed in the "Initial Inventory" column. During the sales period, restocking is not allowed and there is no in-transit inventory.

Demand for the "4U" products during the sales horizon is assumed to be deterministic and known in advance, with demand quantities specified in the "Demand" column. The decision variable x_i represents the number of units of each "4U" product i that the retailer plans to fulfill, where each x_i is a non-negative integer. Because the fulfillment quantity cannot exceed either the available inventory or the realized demand, the decision variables must satisfy both inventory and demand constraints.

The retailer therefore aims to determine the optimal fulfillment quantities in order to maximize total revenue while respecting both inventory availability and demand limits.

A restaurant offers a variety of popular products, including fast food and beverages. The profit data for these products is provided in the "Revenue" column. Each product has its own demand level. The restaurant aims to maximize total revenue by focusing on the initial inventory of products classified under "Aalop" (i.e., items with names containing "Aalop"), which are detailed in the "Initial Inventory" column. During the sales period, restocking is not permitted, and there are no in-transit inventories. Demand for "Aalop"  products during the sales horizon is assumed to be deterministic and known in advance, with demand information specified in the "Demand" column. The variables x_i represent the number of units of each "Aalop" product i that the restaurant intends to fulfill.

A farmer wishes to plan production on his all_space acre farm over the next five years. At present, he has a herd of 120 cows. This is made up of heifers (cows aged 0 and 1) and milk-producing cows (aged 2 and above). `InitialAgeCounts[a]` gives the number of animals of each age at the start of year 1. A maximum of `NMaxCow' cows can be housed at the present time. To provide accommodation for each cow beyond this number will entail a capital outlay of `CowOutlay' per cow. 
Each cow needs a certain number of acres to support it. `AllSpace`, `HeiferSpace`, and `CowSpace` define total land use. A dairy cow can produce a certain number of calves per year. Half of these calves will be bullocks, which are sold almost immediately. The remaining heifers can be either sold almost immediately or reared to become milk-producing cows at two years old. It is intended that all dairy cows be sold at 12 years old, although there will probably be an annual loss of per year among heifers and dairy cows. CowCalve`, `LossHeifer`, and `LossCow` define births and mortality. The milk from a cow yields an annual revenue. `RevenueMilk`, `PriceBullock`, `PriceHeifer`, and `PriceCow` define revenues from milk, bullocks, age-0 heifer sales, and year-end age-11 cow sales. 
Each milk- producing cow require `CowGrain' tons of grain and `CowSugar` tons of sugar beet per year. Grain and sugar beet can both be grown on the farm. Sugar beet yields `SugarPerAcre' tons. Only `SpaceGrain' acres are suitable for growing grain. They can be divided into groups. Group k has space `GrainDivision[k]' and yields `GrainYield' tons per acre. Grain can be bought for `BuyPriceGrain' per ton and sold for `SellPriceGrain' per ton. Sugar beet can be bought for `BuyPriceSugar' per ton and sold for `SellPriceSugar' per ton. 
Each heifer requires `LabourHeifers' hours of labour per year. Each milk-producing cow requires `LabourCow' hours of labour per year. Each acre put into grain requires `LabourGrain' hours of labour per year. Each acre put into sugar beet requires `LabourSugar' hours of labour per year. There are also extra costs. Each heifer requires `ExtraHeifers' per year. Each milk-producing cow requires `ExtraCow' per year. Each acre put into grain requires `ExtraGrain' per year. Each acre put into sugar beet requires `ExtraSugar' per year. Labour costs for the farm are at present `LabourCost' per year and provide `LabourHour' labour. Any labour needed above this will cost `ExtraLabourCost' per hour. Any capital expenditure would be financed by a `LoanTermYears'-year loan at `LoanInterestRate'% annual interest. The interest and capital repayment would be paid in 10 equally sized yearly installments. In no year can the cash flow be negative. Finally, the farmer would neither wish to reduce the total number of dairy cows at the end of the five-year period by more than 50% nor wish to increase the number by more than 75%.

Text Description:
A non-governmental organization (NGO) operates a network of transit monitoring stations along high-risk travel corridors, such as border crossings, bus terminals, and airports, with the goal of identifying and intercepting potential victims of human trafficking before exploitation occurs. At each station, trained staff observe travelers and intervene when individuals exhibit known trafficking risk indicators. However, stations differ substantially in the amount of resources they receive (e.g., number of staff, level of training, and operating intensity) as well as in the outcomes they generate (e.g., number of individuals screened, number of high-risk cases identified, and number of successful interventions). Because of these differences, leadership is interested in evaluating how effectively each station converts its available resources into meaningful anti-trafficking outcomes. 
To support this evaluation, the NGO collects operational data over multiple time periods for each monitoring station. Each station-period pair can be viewed as a unit whose performance depends on several inputs (representing resources and effort) and several outputs (representing different measures of success in identifying and assisting potential victims). The organization recognizes that not all outputs are equally easy to achieve and that stations operate under slightly different environmental conditions, so comparisons must be made carefully among comparable units. The goal is to construct a performance benchmark that identifies which stations are operating efficiently relative to others and quantifies how much improvement is possible for underperforming stations, given the observed practices of their peers. 
You are asked to formulate a model that evaluates the relative efficiency of each station by comparing it to a best-practice frontier formed by other stations in the dataset. The model should determine, for each station, whether its observed combination of resource usage and outcomes can be matched or improved upon by a hypothetical combination of other stations. If not, the station is considered efficient; otherwise, the model should indicate how its performance could be improved (e.g., by increasing certain outcomes or reducing resource usage). The formulation should allow flexibility in how inputs and outputs are weighted, but these weights must be chosen consistently to ensure fair comparisons across all stations. 
Data: We have `J' different stations to evaluate, with `M' different inputs and `N' outputs. We are also given for station j `x_{mj}' the amount of input m from station j, and `y_{nj} the amount of output n from station j. 
The goal is to determine weights, or price multipliers, that optimize an efficiency objective while ensuring that the total weighted input contributions for stations must be at least as large as the total weighted output contributions (so that stations cannot receive more in outputs than is put in). If there exists weights such that the weighted input contribution is equal to the weighted output contribution for the reference station, then this station is considered efficient. First, rescale the station being evaluated so that, after applying the chosen output weights, its total "valued" outputs equal one. Then, using those same weights, require that for every station in the dataset, the total "valued" inputs are at least as large as the total "valued" outputs, after adjusting by the common offset. Finally, choose the weights and the offset to make the evaluated station"s "valued" inputs (after the same adjustment) as small as possible.
Vague Description: We run monitoring stations at transit hubs to identify potential trafficking victims. The stations vary a lot in terms of staff and resources, and also in terms of how many people they screen and how many cases they identify. We want to understand which stations are genuinely performing well relative to what they have to work with, and flag the ones that could be doing better.

Text Description:
We want to optimize the waste collection system for a city, taking full account of the city's particular characteristics. We want to find a collection truck route for each zone and minimize its length while only visiting each garbage collection stop once. The city has a few important rules that need to be integrated into the route: 1. A long block needs to be serviced directly. `L_e[e]` lists the transitions whose underlying paths directly service long block side `e`. 2. We need to respect some important traffic patterns. `V_ij[(i,j)]` is the set of successor stops that cannot follow transition `(i,j)` because doing so would violate a forbidden 3-node traffic pattern. 
Some important data: - `V_T` is the set of stops where waste needs to be collected in the zone. - Moving from stop `i` to stop `j` means traversing a precomputed shortest path in the underlying street network. - `ell[i][j]` is the length of the quickest trip between stop i and j. - Stop `s` is the departure node and stop `t` must be the last service node visited before returning to `s`.
Vague Description: We need to plan a route for a garbage truck through a neighborhood so every stop gets serviced and the total driving distance is minimized. There are some local rules — certain streets need to be driven along directly, and some turns aren't allowed — that make it more complicated than a simple loop.

Improving fulfillment efficiency is critical for long-term sustainability of online grocery retailing. We want to reduce order fulfillment cost by order consolidation. Motivated by the observation that a significant percentage of buyers place multiple orders within a short time interval, we want a scheme that attempts to consolidate such "multiorders" to reduce the number of parcels and hence, the shipping cost. A multiorder is a set of two or more orders that satisfy the following criteria: (1) placed by the same buyer, (2) placed on the same day, (3) have the same delivery address, (4) assigned to the same fulfillment center (FC), and (5) satisfy the free shipping requirements. Multiorders can be consolidated into a single parcel, reducing shipping costs. A hit, or multiorder hit, occurs when a new order arrives that can be consolidated with an existing order in the pool, forming a multiorder. Capturing a hit means successfully identifying and consolidating these orders, resulting in cost savings. 
We have created buckets of items with different probabilities of turning into multi orders. `K` probability buckets are used, with representative multiorder probabilities `p[k]`. We have designed prediction models that forecast the amount of order arrivals that arrive for each of time period `¦Ó' (through the end of the horizon `T'). `I[¦Ó]` is the bucketed arrival forecast. We also have a model that predicts which fraction of arrival will land in each bucket `k', `arrival_shares[k]`. We have also forecasted epsilon[¦Ó][s][k]`, the number of bucket-`k` orders that arrived in period `s` and are cleared as multiorder hits in period `¦Ó`. In practice these are stochastic, but for our model we will assume our forecasting models are perfect and use the data as ground-truth. 
There are some operational constraints on the problem. An order may stay in the pool a maximum of `L' days, and we may have at most a pool size of `C[¦Ó]` at the end of each time period (after orders have been released). We can also release at most `F_bar[¦Ó]` units per time period. There is a per-unit penalty of `c_F[¦Ó]` for violating that cap. Our goal is to maximize the probability weighted amount of inventory carried forward (to maximize chances of multi-orders) minus the cost of exceeding the release limits (assume `c_F[¦Ó]' is already weighted and in the same units so we don't need to balance the objective terms). The pool starts empty and must be empty at the end of the horizon.

We want to decide which orders to hold and when to send them out. We can't hold them too long, and we don't want to release too many at once, but we also can't leave orders sitting at the end of the day.
